## 4. Sessions and reconstruction

### 4.1 Definition

A **context** is `(app, normalized window title)`: a document in an editor, a
Chrome tab, a terminal tab, a chat conversation. A **session** is a run of
writing in one context:

- It **starts** with the first `key` event in a context that has no open
  session. Focus changes alone never create sessions, so rapid Alt-Tab
  cycling produces nothing.
- It **ends** when either:
  1. **Idle:** 30 s pass with no keystroke *in that context*.
     `ended_at` = its last keystroke; or
  2. **Commit:** Enter (without Shift) in a **single-line context**: terminal
     prompts, chat compose boxes, the browser address bar. The Enter is the
     last event of the session.
- **Focus loss does not end a session.** Switching away to look something up
  and coming back within 30 s of the context's *own* last keystroke resumes
  the same session. Several contexts can have open sessions at the same time,
  each with its own idle clock.

Why: the assignment's queries are about *intent* ("what did I tell Dana",
"which command did I run"). One chat message or one shell command is a natural
unit, hence commit-on-Enter where Enter means "send". For long-form editing, a
pause of half a minute is a good boundary between bursts of writing, and the
per-context clock keeps a quick glance at another window from fragmenting a
paragraph. A fixed time grid or "one session per focus span" would split
sentences across alt-tabs and merge unrelated work.

### 4.2 Text across sessions

Each context keeps a **running text buffer** that persists across its
sessions. A session's stored text is **the buffer state when the session
closes**. This gives exactly the search semantics the assignment asks for:

- A word typed and deleted inside one session is gone by the close, so that
  session is not findable by it.
- A word present at the close stays in that session's stored text forever,
  even if a *later* session in the same context deletes it.

For single-line contexts, a commit stores the line and then clears the buffer
(the shell prompt or chat box is empty again). After a restart, a context's
buffer is seeded from the text of its most recent closed session (section
4.5), with the cursor at the end.

### 4.3 State machine (per context)

```
                    key in ctx
      ┌────────┐ ─────────────────► ┌──────────────┐
      │  IDLE  │                    │    OPEN      │◄──┐ key in ctx
      │(buffer │ ◄───────────────── │ (session s)  │───┘ (refresh last_key_ts)
      │ kept)  │  idle 30s: close s │              │
      └────────┘  commit-Enter:     └──────┬───────┘
          ▲       close s (+clear          │ focus away / back: no transition
          │       buffer if single-line)   │ caption change → different ctx
          └────────────────────────────────┘
```

Idle closure is decided **from log timestamps** (the next key in the context is
> 30 s after the last one, or the log has no further events and the wall clock
is > 30 s past it). The wall clock only decides *when* ingest flushes a closed
session, never *what* it contains, so replaying the same log always gives the
same sessions.

### 4.4 Reconstruction ladder

Keys are not text, so reconstruction is tiered by how much is known about the
app:

- **Tier 0: generic buffer replay (all apps).** A virtual buffer with a
  cursor and an optional selection. It handles printable characters (replacing
  the selection), Enter/Tab, Backspace/Delete, Left/Right/Up/Down, Home/End,
  Ctrl+Backspace / Ctrl+Delete / Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right as word operations,
  Shift+arrows selection, Ctrl+A select-all, and paste. On Ctrl+V or
  Shift+Insert, the ingest thread fetches the current clipboard text from
  KDE's Klipper over D-Bus and inserts it. Paste is resolved at capture time
  and the clipboard text written into the log as a field of the paste event,
  since the clipboard may have changed by the time ingest runs. **After a
  `click`, the cursor position is unknown and the cursor snaps to the end of
  the buffer.** This is a documented limitation: editing in the middle of text
  after a mouse click lands in the wrong place.
- **Tier 1: static per-app rules on top of tier 0.** A small explicit table
  keyed by app id:
  - *Terminals* (`org.kde.konsole`, `kitty`, `Alacritty`, `org.wezfurlong.wezterm`,
    `foot`, `gnome-terminal`, `xterm`…): readline/zle keys. Ctrl+U kills to
    line start, Ctrl+W kills the previous word, Ctrl+A / Ctrl+E go to line
    start/end (*not* select-all), Ctrl+C abandons the line (buffer cleared, no
    commit), Ctrl+Shift+V pastes. Enter commits.
  - *Chat apps* (`slack`, `discord`, `org.telegram.desktop`, `signal`…):
    Enter commits, Shift+Enter inserts a newline.
  - *Browsers* (`google-chrome`, `chromium`, `firefox`…): Ctrl+L, Alt+D, F6 or
    Ctrl+T open an *address-bar sub-context*. Its keystrokes go to a separate
    single-line buffer, and Enter commits it as its own session (this is how
    "what did I search for" stays separate from text typed into the page).
  - Editors: Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y are *not* modelled (the undo history isn't
    observable). This is noted as a source of divergence.
- **Tier 2: real-app replay for VS Code (opt-in, `brain run --vscode-replay`).**
  When a VS Code session closes, its keystrokes are replayed over the Chrome
  DevTools Protocol (`Input.dispatchKeyEvent`) into a warm, hidden VS Code
  instance on Xvfb. The instance has a snapshot of the file taken at session
  start, so autocomplete, auto-closing brackets, auto-indent and multi-cursor
  behave as they did for the user, and the resulting document is read back.
  Constraints:
  - It requires the user to set `window.title` to include
    `${activeEditorLong}`, so the caption carries the file path.
  - The replay instance is network-isolated (no network namespace access),
    resource-capped in its own cgroup (`systemd-run --user --scope` with
    memory and CPU limits), runs one replay at a time, and is killed on
    timeout. Any failure falls back to the tier-0 result.
  - It runs only *after* a session closes, never on the hot path. Its memory
    and CPU are outside brain's own budget but are real costs on the user's
    machine, which is why it is off by default.
  - Chrome and terminals stay at tiers 0/1. Sandboxed replay designs for those
    (headless Chromium with the page snapshot, a pty running the user's shell
    in a throwaway namespace) are future work: replaying shell input carries
    the risk of re-executing commands, which needs a much stronger sandbox
    than an editor does.

### 4.5 Restart with open sessions

On startup, ingest replays from `ingest_state.log_offset` (the resume point,
3.3). When it first sees a context at byte offset `o`, it seeds that context's
buffer from the stored text of the latest closed session of the context with
`end_offset < o` (empty if none, or if that session ended by commit in a
single-line context). From there, normal processing applies. Sessions that had
already closed during the replayed span are recomputed with the same ids and
upserted unchanged. Sessions that were open at the kill become open again and
close on their own timestamps.

### 4.6 Edge cases

- **Title churn.** Captions change without the user switching context. Before
  they form a context key, captions are normalized by:
  - stripping editor dirty markers (leading `●`, `*`, `• `; trailing
    ` - Modified`, `[+]`, `(modified)`),
  - stripping leading unread counters such as `(3) ` (Gmail, Slack, Discord),
  - stripping the trailing app suffix (` - Google Chrome`, ` — Konsole`,
    ` - Visual Studio Code`), which carries no information because the app id
    is already in the key.
  The raw caption is still logged in `focus` events.
- **Real context switches inside one window.** A Chrome tab switch or a VS
  Code file switch changes the caption, so it is a new context with its own
  session and buffer. That is the intent.
- **Terminal titles that track the running command.** Konsole's title changes
  when a command starts (`vim foo — Konsole`). Enter has already committed the
  prompt's session, so nothing is split. Typing inside `vim` is a different
  context, which is correct.
- **Rapid Alt-Tab.** Produces `focus` lines only. No sessions, no buffer
  changes.
- **Keystrokes before the first focus report**, or while KWin is restarting:
  tagged `unknown`, reconstructed as their own context.
- **Idle across sleep.** Wall-clock time advances during suspend, so the
  first keystroke after resume is > 30 s after the previous one and the
  session closes, as wanted. Repeat timers are cancelled before sleep, so a
  key held at suspend time cannot repeat forever on resume.
- **Clock changes / NTP steps.** Logged timestamps are wall time (that is what
  `--at` and `--from/--to` mean to a user). A backward step counts as a zero
  gap (no split). A forward step > 30 s splits the session, which is
  harmless. Timestamps stay in log order for sessionizing; checkpoints and
  `query text` handle non-monotonic stretches conservatively (section 5.4).
- **Screen locked.** No key events are written, so the password is never seen.
  The session's idle clock keeps running and it closes after 30 s.
- **Passwords elsewhere** (sudo prompts, browser login forms) cannot be
  distinguished at the key level. See section 8.
- **`run` restarted** while sessions are open: section 4.5.
- **Unbounded buffers.** Each context buffer is capped (e.g. 64 KiB, oldest
  text dropped). Contexts idle for hours are evicted from memory, and
  reseeding from SQLite (4.5) restores them on demand, so memory is bounded
  regardless of how many windows were used.

---

## 5. Storage and indexing

### 5.1 Layout

```
brain-data/            (0700)
  lock                 flock target, prevents two `run`s
  events.jsonl         append-only ground truth (0600)
  brain.db, -wal, -shm SQLite index, derived and rebuildable (0600)
```

### 5.2 Schema

```sql
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous  = NORMAL;   -- index is rebuildable; log carries durability
PRAGMA cache_size   = -2000;    -- ~2 MB page cache

CREATE TABLE sessions (
  id           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,      -- 's-<start byte offset>', deterministic
  app          TEXT NOT NULL,
  context      TEXT NOT NULL,         -- normalized window title
  started_at   INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- unix ms, first keystroke
  ended_at     INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- unix ms, last keystroke
  start_offset INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- log byte offsets of first/last event
  end_offset   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  close_reason TEXT NOT NULL,         -- 'idle' | 'commit'
  tier         INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- reconstruction tier that produced text
  text         TEXT NOT NULL          -- buffer state at close
);
CREATE INDEX sessions_app_time ON sessions(app, ended_at);
CREATE INDEX sessions_ctx      ON sessions(app, context, end_offset);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE sessions_fts USING fts5(
  text, content='sessions', content_rowid='rowid',
  tokenize='porter unicode61'
);
-- External-content FTS: the text is stored once (in sessions), FTS stores
-- only the inverted index. Triggers keep it in sync atomically.
CREATE TRIGGER sessions_ai AFTER INSERT ON sessions BEGIN
  INSERT INTO sessions_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER sessions_ad AFTER DELETE ON sessions BEGIN
  INSERT INTO sessions_fts(sessions_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.text);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER sessions_au AFTER UPDATE ON sessions BEGIN
  INSERT INTO sessions_fts(sessions_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.text);
  INSERT INTO sessions_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;

CREATE TABLE ingest_state (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1),
  log_offset INTEGER NOT NULL       -- resume point (section 3.3)
);

CREATE TABLE log_checkpoints (
  app         TEXT NOT NULL,
  ts          INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- unix ms
  byte_offset INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- offset of a line boundary at/before ts
  PRIMARY KEY (app, ts)
);
```

Raw keystrokes are **not** copied into SQLite. The log already holds them, and
duplicating them would double the write volume and the disk usage for no
query that needs it (`query text` reads the log directly via checkpoints).

### 5.3 Why SQLite + WAL + FTS5

| Option | Concurrency with a live writer | Crash safety | Full-text | Footprint | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SQLite WAL + FTS5** | One writer, any number of readers, readers never block and see a snapshot | Atomic transactions; recovery on open | Built in: tokenizers, AND queries, `snippet()`, bm25 | ~1 MB library, configurable cache | **Chosen** |
| tantivy | Single writer, readers on committed segments; works well | Commit-based, good | Excellent, richer query language | Heavier: indexing buffers ≥ several MB, segment merges, larger binary | Overkill for kB-sized sessions; budget risk under 32 MB |
| Custom inverted index | Whatever we build | Whatever we build (and must test) | Whatever we build | Smallest possible | Reinvents transactions + snapshot isolation; that's where the bugs would be |
| Plain files + grep at query time | Trivially safe to read | Append-only is safe | Linear scan; no word semantics without our own tokenizer | Minimal | Fine at day 1, degrades linearly; no snapshot of session state |

The deciding property is **snapshot isolation under a live writer**, which the
assignment demands ("always sees a consistent state"). In WAL mode, a reader's
transaction sees the database as of its first read, no matter how many commits
happen meanwhile. SQLite provides this out of the box and has been tested at
scale.

### 5.4 Tokenizer and its implications

`porter unicode61`: unicode61 splits on Unicode word boundaries, case-folds,
and removes diacritics, so search is case-insensitive as required. `porter`
then stems English words.

- **Effect:** `migration` matches `migrations` and `migrating`. For a recall
  tool ("what did I tell Dana about the migration?") that is usually what the
  user wants. It is a deliberate loosening of the literal "all words must
  appear".
- **Prefix search** (`migr*`) is not exposed. Query words are quoted before
  being passed to FTS5 (`"migration" "dana"`), so user input can never inject
  FTS syntax (`OR`, `NEAR`, `*`, column filters). A `prefix='2 3'` index could
  add it later at some index-size cost.
- Code-like tokens (`snake_case`, `foo.bar()`) split on punctuation, so
  searching `foo bar` finds `foo.bar`. Non-English text works but is not
  stemmed.

### 5.5 Checkpoints and history (`--at`)

`log_checkpoints` maps `(app, time) → byte offset of a line boundary`. Ingest
writes a row per app every few seconds of activity, in the same transaction as
everything else. To read the log for an app between `from` and `to`, a query
finds the greatest checkpoint with `ts ≤ from` (any app's checkpoint is a valid
seek point, because the log is a single append-only stream), seeks there, and
scans forward to the first event with `ts > to` plus a small slack, to tolerate
small backward clock steps. Seeking is O(log n). The scan is bounded by the
window size, not the history size.

### 5.6 Consistency for concurrent readers

`brain query` opens the database read-only and does all of the following
inside **one read transaction**:

1. Read `ingest_state.log_offset` (= `L`).
2. Run the FTS query over closed sessions.
3. Read the log from `L` to the last complete line at the moment of reading,
   and run tier-0/1 reconstruction to obtain the sessions not yet in the
   snapshot (open ones, or closed but not yet committed). Sessions whose
   deterministic id already exists in the snapshot are skipped, which covers
   the span between the resume point and the read head.

The snapshot plus the log tail form a consistent cut: every event before the
cut is accounted for exactly once, either in a committed session or in the
just-in-time reconstruction. Results remain correct even when `run` is not
running and has left an un-ingested tail.

### 5.7 Growth and retention

About 100 bytes per logged keystroke. A heavy day of 50,000 keystrokes is
~5 MB of log. Sessions add the final text once, plus FTS postings (~1–2× the
text). Expected growth is low single-digit MB per day, about 1 GB per year at
heavy use. Planned retention (not in the first version): rotate the log into
segment files named by their starting global offset (so offsets stay global
and checkpoints stay valid), and add `brain prune --before T`, which deletes
segments and the corresponding sessions in one step.

---

## 6. Query semantics

All output is JSON on stdout. Errors (bad arguments, unparseable time, missing
data dir, unreadable database) go to stderr with a non-zero exit code. Times
accept RFC 3339 (`2026-11-08T14:03:22Z`, with offset) or local
`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]`, interpreted in the local time zone. Output times are
UTC RFC 3339 with milliseconds.

### 6.1 `brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--limit N]`

- Words are split on whitespace and each one is quoted; all must match (FTS5
  implicit AND) within one session's text. Matching is case-insensitive and
  stemmed (5.4).
- `--app`: exact app id. `--from/--to`: the session's `[started_at,
  ended_at]` overlaps the range. `--limit`: default 20.
- Sources: closed sessions via `sessions_fts`, plus **open / un-ingested
  sessions** reconstructed just in time from the log tail (5.6). To make those
  match with *identical* semantics, their texts are loaded into a temporary
  in-memory FTS5 table with the same tokenizer and the same query runs over
  it. No second tokenizer is implemented in Rust.
- Ordering: most recent `ended_at` first. bm25 scores from two different FTS
  tables are not comparable, and recency suits the "what did I write about X"
  use case.
- `snippet` comes from FTS5 `snippet()` with `…` ellipses around the first
  matching region.

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "session_id": "s-18234011",
      "app": "slack",
      "started_at": "2026-11-08T14:03:21.950Z",
      "ended_at": "2026-11-08T14:09:51.004Z",
      "snippet": "…the migration is blocked on the schema change…"
    }
  ]
}
```

For an open session, `ended_at` is its latest keystroke so far.

### 6.2 `brain query text --app A [--at T] [--from T --to T]`

Returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** for the app over a time window:
printable characters exactly as captured, in order, with Enter → `\n` and
Tab → `\t`. Backspace, cursor movement and shortcuts (any key with
Ctrl/Alt/Super) are **not** applied or emitted.

- No time flags: the last 10 minutes.
- `--at T`: the 10-minute window ending at `T`.
- `--from/--to`: an explicit window.
- Covers all windows of that app. Reads the log directly (seeking via
  checkpoints), so it includes events not yet ingested.

```json
{ "app": "org.kde.konsole", "at": "2026-11-08T14:10:00.000Z", "text": "git sttus\ngit status\nkubectl get pods -n prod\n" }
```

`at` is `null` when `--at` was not given.

**Decision and trade-off.** The assignment says `text` "returns current text,
or its text at time T", which can be read as *reconstructed* text (the edited
buffer). We return the raw stream on purpose:

- It is lossless and never wrong. Reconstruction can drift (mouse clicks,
  autocomplete, undo); the raw stream cannot.
- It answers "what did I do" questions (which command did I run, what did I
  try first) that edited text erases. Typos and corrected attempts are
  information.
- Edit-aware text is already what `search` indexes. Having both views means
  neither one hides the other.

The cost: a reader expecting the final document sees typos and keystrokes that
were later deleted, and text deleted by Backspace still appears. An edit-aware
"buffer state of each context at T" view is cheap to add on the same
machinery (replay the context's buffer to `T`) and is listed as future work.

---

## 7. Resource budget

Targets: no input lag, ≤ 1% average CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB memory.

**No input lag by construction.** brain is a passive evdev reader, not on the
delivery path (2.2). Nothing it does, including stalling completely, can delay
a keystroke reaching the compositor.

**CPU.**

- No async runtime. The capture thread is one `epoll` loop over evdev fds, the
  inotify fd, the repeat `timerfd` and the fsync `timerfd`. It sleeps in
  `epoll_wait` between events: no polling, no busy timers.
- Per keystroke: one `read()` of a few `input_event`s, an xkbcommon state
  update and keysym lookup (sub-µs), JSON formatting into a reused buffer, and
  one `write()` (~1–5 µs into the page cache). At a fast ~10 keystrokes/s that
  is well under 100 µs of CPU per second: < 0.01% of a core. Holding a key
  (25 Hz repeat) is within the same order.
- `fdatasync` at most once per second while typing.
- Ingest wakes per durable-offset bump (≤ 1/s) and does one small SQLite
  transaction. FTS work per session is proportional to the session's text
  (bytes to kB).
- D-Bus: zbus's blocking API (it runs a small internal executor thread). There
  is traffic only on focus/caption changes.
- The KWin script is event-driven inside KWin and does no work between window
  events.

**Memory.**

- No tokio. Three threads plus zbus's internal one, with small stacks.
- SQLite `cache_size` ~2 MB, no mmap, one connection on the writer side.
- Context buffers capped and evicted (4.6). The repeat and sessionizer state
  is O(open contexts).
- Expected steady-state RSS: low single-digit MB for capture, plus a few MB
  for SQLite and zbus. Comfortably under 32 MB, and asserted in tests (below).

**How it is verified.**

- A perf harness generates keystrokes through a virtual keyboard
  (`evemu-play` or a tiny uinput program; only the *generator* needs uinput
  access, brain runs unprivileged) at 10 keys/s with realistic Backspace and
  focus changes for 10 minutes. It samples brain's `utime+stime` from
  `/proc/<pid>/stat` and `VmRSS`/`VmHWM` from `/proc/<pid>/status`, and fails
  if average CPU > 1% or peak RSS > 32 MB.
- Latency: the same harness compares evdev timestamps with logged timestamps
  (they must be identical, because the kernel stamp is propagated), and
  measures write-to-ingest delay.
- `perf stat` / `strace -c` spot checks to confirm one `write()` per event and
  no stray wake-ups while idle.

---

## 8. Security and privacy

A keystroke logger is sensitive software by definition. The design keeps the
blast radius small:

- **Data at rest.** `brain-data/` is created 0700 and its files 0600.
  Everything stays local; there is no network code in `brain` at all. (The
  opt-in VS Code replay instance is network-isolated too.)
- **Passwords.**
  - The screen locker is handled explicitly: capture pauses while
    `ScreenSaver.ActiveChanged` reports locked.
  - Other password prompts (sudo in a terminal, web logins, polkit dialogs)
    cannot be recognized from key events. Mitigations: a configurable app
    denylist (e.g. password managers, `org.kde.polkit-kde-authentication-agent-1`),
    whose keys are logged with the character replaced by a placeholder.
    Terminal sudo prompts remain a known exposure. AT-SPI's `password text`
    role would be the principled fix (section 10).
- **Clipboard.** Paste content is fetched from Klipper *only on a paste
  keystroke* and stored, because it is part of what was written. Copying
  alone is never recorded.
- **Privilege.** brain runs as the user and needs read access to
  `/dev/input/event*` only, not root, not uinput. The README documents that
  `input` group membership grants this to all of the user's processes, and
  offers a narrower udev ACL rule as an alternative.
- **Compositor integration.** The KWin script only reads window metadata and
  calls one D-Bus method. It cannot inject input.
- **Query injection.** Search words are always quoted before reaching FTS5,
  and every SQL statement uses bound parameters.

---

## 9. Testing strategy

- **Pluggable event source.** Capture is split into a `KeySource` (evdev in
  production) and a pure *decoder* (xkb state + repeat synthesis + JSON).
  Tests feed recorded or scripted `input_event` sequences with explicit
  timestamps and assert on the exact JSONL produced: shift/caps handling,
  shared modifier state across two keyboards, Ctrl+A → `"a"` + `ctrl`, repeat
  timing, `SYN_DROPPED` resync.
- **Reconstruction and sessions as pure functions of the log.** Golden tests
  map JSONL fixtures to expected sessions/text. They cover:
  - typed-then-deleted words,
  - deletion in a later session,
  - Ctrl+Backspace, select-all + type, terminal Ctrl+U/W, chat Shift+Enter vs
    Enter,
  - address-bar sub-contexts,
  - click → cursor snaps to end,
  - title normalization (`●`, `(3) `),
  - focus away and back within / after 30 s,
  - backward and forward clock steps.
  Property tests check that splitting a log at any byte offset and resuming
  (the restart path) produces the same sessions as one pass.
- **Crash test.** A loop that runs `brain run` on a replay source, sends
  `kill -9` at random moments (including mid-ingest-transaction, forced with a
  test hook that sleeps inside the transaction), restarts, and finally checks:
  - `PRAGMA integrity_check` passes,
  - no torn lines remain,
  - the sessions table equals a from-scratch rebuild of the same log,
  - no event present in the log is missing from the derived state.
- **Concurrent query consistency.** While ingest commits continuously, many
  `brain query` processes run in parallel. Each asserts that every event up to
  its observed log end is accounted for exactly once (no duplicate or missing
  session between the snapshot and the tail), and that no query ever fails
  with `SQLITE_BUSY`.
- **Perf harness.** Section 7 (CPU ≤ 1%, RSS ≤ 32 MB), run in CI-like
  fashion on the dev machine.
- **Sleep/wake simulation.** Invoke the `PrepareForSleep(true/false)` handlers
  directly. In integration, use a fake logind on a private D-Bus (or
  `systemctl suspend` manually). Also simulate device loss with `ENODEV` from
  the fake source, and check that devices reopen, the xkb state resets and the
  KWin script is re-registered.
- **Manual end-to-end checklist** on Plasma Wayland: Konsole, Chrome, VS Code,
  a Slack/Electron app, XWayland app, USB keyboard hotplug, lock/unlock,
  suspend/resume, `kill -9` during typing.

---

## 10. Risks, known limitations and future work

| Area | Limitation | Impact | Future work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fidelity | Keys, not text: autocomplete, auto-pairing, undo, drag-and-drop, IME are invisible to tier 0/1 | Reconstructed text can diverge from the real document, mostly in editors | Tier 2 for VS Code (opt-in); AT-SPI as a correcting second source for GTK/Qt; editor/browser extensions where exactness matters |
| Cursor | After a mouse click the cursor position is unknown → snap to end | Mid-text edits after clicking land in the wrong place | AT-SPI caret events; per-app extensions |
| Keymap | Single layout from `kxkbrc`; runtime layout switching, compose and dead keys not interpreted | Wrong characters for multi-layout users / accented input | Follow KDE layout D-Bus signals; xkbcommon compose tables |
| Platform | KDE Plasma only (Wayland and X11) | GNOME/wlroots users can't attribute focus | GNOME Shell extension; `wlr-foreign-toplevel-management` backend for Sway/Hyprland |
| Privacy | Passwords outside the lock screen can't be recognized | Secrets typed in terminals/web forms are logged | AT-SPI `password text` detection; app denylist; encrypted log at rest |
| Security | `input` group exposes all keyboards to all user processes | System-level exposure beyond brain | udev ACL scoped to the user/session; document trade-off |
| Sessions | 30 s idle and the single-line app table are heuristics | Some chats/editors split or merge unexpectedly | Make thresholds and the app table configurable; learn from data |
| `query text` | Raw stream rather than edited text | Contains typos and deleted characters | Add an edit-aware "buffer at T" view |
| Tier 2 | Requires `${activeEditorLong}` in VS Code title; heavy external process | Only usable by users who opt in and configure it | Sandboxed replay for Chromium and terminals |
| Storage | Single growing log; no retention yet | ~1 GB/year at heavy use | Segmented log + `brain prune` |
| Search | Stemming loosens "word must appear"; no prefix search | Rare false positives; no partial-word queries | Optional unstemmed column / prefix index |
| Clock | Wall-clock timestamps; large backward steps reorder time | `--at` near a step may miss or include a few seconds | Also log a monotonic/boot-time counter for ordering |
